title: Maine Coon Grooming Guide: Brushing, Shedding & Mats
description: Build a workable Maine Coon grooming routine for brushing, shedding, mats, bathing, nails and coat care.
html:
By Sami, Founder of Wise Maine Coon

This guide provides general education and does not replace advice from your veterinarian or a qualified feline groomer.

Most cats can begin a Maine Coon grooming routine with two or three thorough combing sessions each week, plus a quick daily check of areas where mats form easily. A cottony or tangle-prone coat, heavy seasonal shedding, reduced self-grooming, or existing knots may make daily grooming necessary.

The goal is not to follow one rigid schedule. It is to keep a comb moving gently through the coat down to the skin, notice small knots before they become painful mats, and make handling feel safe. This guide explains the schedule, essential tools, brushing method, shedding care, occasional bathing, and warning signs that need professional help.


How Often Should You Groom a Maine Coon?

The Cat Fanciers’ Association recommends combing a Maine Coon two or three times a week. That is a practical starting point for a healthy adult whose coat stays smooth between sessions. A full session can take only five to ten minutes when knots are found early.

Add a 30–60 second daily check behind the ears, under the front legs, along the belly, between the back legs and around the britches. A check is not the same as a complete grooming session: use your fingers to feel for a new knot, damp patch, debris or sensitive area, then schedule a proper comb-through if you find one.

Coat texture matters. TICA notes that some Maine Coons have a silky coat that needs less attention, while cottony coats can require daily combing. Increase grooming during heavy shedding and whenever loose undercoat begins to collect. Kittens benefit from short handling practice; seniors, overweight cats and cats with limited mobility may need more hands-on help.

A starting Maine Coon grooming schedule
Task Starting schedule Adjust when
Check mat-prone areas Daily You find a knot, debris, moisture or tenderness
Full comb and brush 2–3 times weekly Daily for cottony coats, heavy shedding or repeated tangles
Nail check and trim Check weekly; trim as needed Nails snag, become sharply hooked or grow toward the pad
Bath Occasionally, when genuinely needed The coat is dirty or greasy, or a professional gives a specific plan
Skin and coat check During every session You see bald areas, sores, parasites, pain or a sudden change

This schedule is a starting framework, not veterinary instruction for every cat.


Maine Coon Grooming Tools You Actually Need

The best brush for a Maine Coon is not one universal product. A brush helps lift loose hair and finish the surface, while a long-toothed metal comb reaches through the coat and reveals hidden resistance. If the comb cannot pass gently through a section, the coat is not yet tangle-free there.

Essential Maine Coon grooming tools
Tool Main job Safe-use note
Long-toothed stainless-steel comb Find hidden tangles and comb through the full coat Use gently and stop instead of dragging through resistance
Wide-toothed comb Make the first pass through dense areas or small loose tangles Work from the hair ends inward, not from the skin outward
Soft slicker or pin brush Collect loose fur and smooth the coat Use light pressure; do not repeatedly scrape one area
Cat nail clippers Remove sharp nail tips Avoid the pink quick and ask for a demonstration if unsure
Cat-safe shampoo Clean the coat during an occasional bath Never substitute human or baby shampoo
Towel and non-slip mat Provide stable footing and controlled drying Keep the room warm and dry the dense coat thoroughly


Avoid scissors, razors, essential oils, human detanglers, and human shampoo. A strong deshedding blade can also remove or damage more coat than intended when used aggressively. If you want to use a specialized undercoat tool, ask a veterinarian or feline groomer to recommend one for your cat’s coat and demonstrate light, limited use.

How to Brush a Maine Coon Step by Step

  1. Choose a calm moment. Use a stable, non-slip surface and begin when your cat is relaxed rather than playful, hungry, or already irritated.
  2. Introduce the tool. Let the cat sniff the comb, reward calm contact and start with an area the cat already enjoys having touched.
  3. Check with your fingers. Feel through the coat before brushing so you do not pull a hidden knot unexpectedly.
  4. Work in small sections. Follow the direction of hair growth. Begin at the ends of long hair and gradually move closer to the skin.
  5. Support near a small tangle. Hold the fur close to the skin without pinching it, reducing how much the skin moves as you loosen the outer edge.
  6. Verify with the metal comb. Comb down to the skin without scraping it. Stop if you meet firm resistance rather than forcing the teeth through.
  7. Cover high-risk areas. Check the ears, collar line, armpits, ruff, belly, groin, britches and tail base.
  8. Finish gently. Use the soft brush to collect loosened hair, then reward the cat and end before patience runs out.

The five-minute version: check behind the ears and through the ruff, then the armpits, belly and groin, britches and tail base. Finish with a quick comb through the back and sides. On a busy day, checking the places that mat first is more useful than brushing only the easy surface hair.

Where Maine Coons Mat Most Often

Mats form where loose undercoat, moisture and friction meet or where the cat cannot groom effectively. Feel behind the ears and under the collar, beneath the front legs, through the chest ruff, across the belly and groin, between the back legs, around the britches and sanitary area, and near the base of the tail.

Do not rely only on appearance. Long topcoat can hide a knot close to the skin. Part the coat with your fingers and use the comb gently in small sections. A suddenly sensitive area deserves attention even if you cannot see a mat.


How to Handle Tangles and Mats Safely

Small, loose tangles

Hold the hair near the skin so the knot does not pull with every movement. Separate the outer edges gently with your fingers, then use a wide-toothed comb from the hair ends toward the skin. Work for a few seconds at a time and pause if the cat becomes tense.

Stop when the skin moves sharply, the cat shows pain or the tangle does not loosen easily. A small knot is not worth turning grooming into a struggle or causing skin injury.

Tight or skin-level mats

Safety warning: Never cut a mat with scissors. A cat’s thin skin can be pulled into the mat and cut even when the skin is not visible.

Do not repeatedly rake, pull or soak a tight mat. Ask a qualified cat groomer or veterinarian to remove tight, widespread, wet, foul-smelling or painful mats. Choose a groomer with feline-handling experience. A veterinarian should assess mats over red or damaged skin, as well as cases involving sores, parasites, behavior changes or a sudden decline in self-grooming. Decisions about sedation belong to a veterinarian.

Managing Maine Coon Shedding and Hairballs

Maine Coon shedding varies with coat texture, indoor environment and season. Increase gentle combing when loose undercoat accumulates, but do not expect grooming to stop shedding. The practical aim is to remove some loose hair before it tangles or is swallowed during self-grooming.

That may reduce hairball formation, but repeated hacking or vomiting should not automatically be dismissed as “just hairballs.” Cornell advises prompt veterinary assessment when a cat repeatedly retches without producing a hairball, becomes lethargic or stops eating. Contact your veterinarian as well for bald patches, inflamed skin, intense itching, sudden excessive shedding, a greasy or rapidly matting coat, or reduced self-grooming.

Grooming does not make a cat hypoallergenic or eliminate allergens. Clean loose hair from bedding and favorite resting places, but be cautious of products promising to end shedding completely.

Do Maine Coons Need Baths?

Most pet Maine Coons do not need a compulsory monthly bath. Healthy adult cats usually groom themselves effectively, and the need for bathing varies with health, lifestyle and coat condition. An occasional bath may be useful when the coat is genuinely dirty, greasy or contaminated, or when a veterinarian or feline groomer recommends one.

Comb out loose hair and minor tangles before wetting the coat because water can tighten existing knots. Place a non-slip mat in a warm room, use lukewarm water and apply only shampoo formulated for cats. Keep water away from the ears, rinse until no product remains and dry the dense coat thoroughly.

Do not force a frightened cat through a bath. A professional may be safer if the cat panics, the coat cannot be dried properly or medical skin care requires a specific product and schedule.

Nail, Ear and Sanitary Care

Nails

Check every nail weekly and trim the sharp translucent tip only when needed. Avoid the pink quick, which contains blood vessels and nerves. Ask your veterinary team or groomer to demonstrate if you cannot see the quick clearly or your cat resists paw handling. Polydactyl Maine Coons have extra toes, and every extra nail needs inspection because some do not wear down normally.

Ears

Look at the visible outer ear during grooming. Do not insert cotton swabs into the canal or pour in a product that your veterinarian has not approved. Odor, redness, swelling, pain, dark debris or discharge requires veterinary advice rather than vigorous home cleaning.

Sanitary area

Check the long britches for litter, urine or fecal debris. Gently clean minor surface dirt with a cat-safe method recommended by your veterinary team. If soiling happens repeatedly, investigate the cause and ask an experienced feline groomer about a sanitary trim. Beginners should not use scissors close to skin in this area.

How to Groom a Maine Coon That Hates Brushing

Begin with comfortable touch before introducing a tool. Pair one or two gentle strokes along the shoulder or back with a high-value reward, then stop. Keep the first sessions under a minute and end while the cat is still calm.

Build duration gradually and add sensitive areas later; do not begin with the belly or armpits. Several short sessions are safer and more productive than pinning, scruffing or forcing the cat through one long session. Watch for a swishing tail, flattened ears, skin twitching, turning toward the tool or attempts to leave.

Persistent pain, sudden aggression or new sensitivity is not simply bad behavior. Pause grooming and arrange veterinary advice, especially if the change occurs alongside reduced movement, appetite changes or a deteriorating coat.

Kitten, Adult and Senior Grooming Differences

Kitten

Use kitten grooming mainly as positive handling practice before the full adult coat develops. Briefly touch the paws and ears, introduce the comb and brush one calm area, reward cooperation and finish early. The aim is trust, not a perfect coat at every practice session.

Adult

Use the two-to-three-times-weekly baseline and adjust it for texture, season, body condition and lifestyle. An adult with a silky, smooth coat may need less time than one with a dense cottony undercoat, even when both are healthy Maine Coons.

Senior or mobility-limited cat

Increase help in areas the cat can no longer reach easily and keep sessions gentle. Cornell notes that older cats may benefit from more hands-on grooming when self-care declines, but a sudden lack of grooming can indicate a health problem. Arthritis, dental pain, excess weight and illness can all make grooming difficult, so ask your veterinarian about a new or persistent change.

When to Call a Groomer or Veterinarian

A feline-experienced groomer may help A veterinarian should assess
Routine coat maintenance beyond your skill A sudden decline in grooming or painful handling
A safe sanitary trim Redness, sores, odor, discharge or signs of infection
Small-to-moderate mats requiring professional clippers Tight pelting, widespread mats or mats over damaged skin
Bathing and drying an unusually dense coat Bald areas, parasites, excessive itching or unexplained hair loss

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should a Maine Coon be groomed?

Start with two or three thorough combing sessions per week plus quick daily checks of mat-prone areas. Increase the frequency for a cottony coat, heavy shedding, repeated tangles or reduced self-grooming. The right schedule is the one that keeps a comb moving gently through the coat without hidden resistance.

What is the best brush for a Maine Coon?

No single brush suits every coat. A soft slicker or pin brush collects loose surface hair, while a long-toothed metal comb reaches through the coat and finds hidden tangles. Use the comb as the final check and choose gentle tools that do not scrape the skin or pull through resistance.

Can you use a deshedding tool on a Maine Coon?

A specialized undercoat tool may help some heavily shedding coats, but aggressive or repeated use can remove more coat than intended. Ask a veterinarian or feline groomer to recommend a suitable tool and demonstrate light use. A metal comb and soft brush are safer starting tools for most beginners.

How do you remove mats from a Maine Coon?

Small, loose tangles may separate with fingers and a wide-toothed comb worked from the outer end inward while the hair is supported near the skin. Never cut a mat with scissors. Tight, painful, skin-level or widespread mats should be removed by a veterinarian or qualified feline groomer.

Should you shave a Maine Coon in summer?

A healthy, mat-free Maine Coon does not need routine summer shaving merely because the weather is warm. Shaving can expose skin and should not replace coat maintenance. A veterinarian or feline groomer may recommend clipping for severe mats, poor self-grooming or another individual need.

How often should you bathe a Maine Coon?

There is no mandatory monthly schedule for most pet Maine Coons. Bathe occasionally when the coat is genuinely dirty or greasy, or follow a specific veterinary or grooming plan. Remove minor tangles before wetting, use cat-safe shampoo, rinse completely and dry the dense coat in a warm room.

Why is my Maine Coon suddenly getting matted?

A change in shedding, moisture, friction or grooming frequency can cause new mats. Sudden matting can also appear when pain, dental disease, excess weight, limited mobility or illness reduces self-grooming. Arrange veterinary advice when coat deterioration is unexplained, persistent or accompanied by pain, behavior or appetite changes.

A Consistent, Gentle Routine Protects the Coat

A dependable Maine Coon grooming routine begins with two or three full combing sessions each week and fast daily checks of the places that mat first. Use a metal comb to verify the coat down to the skin, keep sessions short and positive, and increase the frequency when your cat’s coat or mobility requires it.

Deal with loose knots early, never place scissors near a mat and seek professional help before tight mats become a painful skin problem. Grooming works best as one part of a complete Maine Coon care routine that also includes nutrition, activity, a suitable home and preventive veterinary care.

About the Author

Sami is the founder and editor of Wise Maine Coon. He researches Maine Coon care using reputable veterinary organizations, breed associations and other authoritative sources.

title: Maine Coon Care Guide: Daily, Weekly & Annual Routine
description: Use this daily, weekly and annual Maine Coon care routine to organize grooming, enrichment, hygiene and preventive care.
html:
By Sami, Founder and Editor of Wise Maine Coon

This article provides general educational information and is not a substitute for veterinary advice. Ask your veterinarian about your cat’s individual diet, preventive care and health needs.


Good Maine Coon care is less about complicated breed-specific rules and more about following a dependable routine. These large, long-haired cats need balanced nutrition, regular coat care, daily activity, appropriately sized equipment and preventive veterinary attention. The exact schedule will vary with your cat’s coat, age, weight, lifestyle and health.

Planning for the years ahead? Read our Maine Coon lifespan guide for life-expectancy data, age stages and health-screening guidance.

If you are considering the breed or caring for one for the first time, this guide organizes the essentials into daily, weekly, monthly and life-stage tasks. It gives you a realistic starting point without treating Maine Coons as either effortless pets or unusually difficult cats.

Quick answer: Maine Coons need the same basic care as other domestic cats, plus consistent combing for their long coat, equipment that safely supports their larger body, daily play, weight monitoring and regular veterinary care. Most routines are manageable when grooming and handling begin early and are adjusted to the individual cat.

Are Maine Coons High Maintenance?

Maine Coons are not exceptionally hard to care for, but they do require consistency. Their size affects practical choices such as carriers, litter boxes, beds and cat trees. Their coat also needs more attention than a typical short-haired cat’s coat.

The amount of grooming is not identical for every Maine Coon. The International Cat Association (TICA) notes that coat texture varies: some cats develop a cottony coat that mats easily, while others have a silkier coat that needs less work. Two or three combing sessions per week are a useful starting point, but an easily tangled coat or heavy seasonal shedding may require more frequent care.

They also need daily play, social interaction and weight monitoring. Their naturally large frame should never be used as a reason to ignore excess body fat. With a predictable routine and equipment chosen for an adult cat’s size, the work is manageable for most prepared owners.

Maine Coon Care at a Glance

The checklist below is a practical starting schedule. Adjust it for your cat’s coat texture, age, health, indoor or outdoor lifestyle, and veterinary advice.

Maine Coon care tasks by frequency
Daily 2–3 times weekly Monthly / as needed Annual / life-stage veterinary care
Serve measured, balanced meals; refresh water; scoop litter; provide play and interaction. Comb the coat; check the belly, legs, chest and behind the ears for tangles; follow the dental routine advised by your veterinarian. Trim nails when needed; check eyes and ears; record weight; inspect the carrier, cat tree and other equipment for wear. Schedule a wellness examination at least annually; schedule senior cats at least every six months. Follow individualized vaccination, parasite-prevention, dental and age-related recommendations.

Feeding and Hydration

A Maine Coon does not need a food simply because the package carries the breed’s name. Choose a cat food labeled complete and balanced for the appropriate life stage, then use the manufacturer’s feeding directions as a starting point. The Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) explains that label directions are guidelines and may need adjustment according to the individual animal’s activity and body condition.

Avoid relying on one universal cup measurement. Two foods can contain very different calories per cup or can, while a cat’s needs change with age, current weight, activity, neuter status and health. Measure portions consistently and account for treats rather than leaving an unlimited amount of calorie-dense food available without monitoring.


For a complete breakdown of food types, portions and feeding schedules, read our Maine Coon food guide.

Because Maine Coons are naturally large, judge condition rather than comparing the number on the scale with that of an average cat. Ask your veterinary team to demonstrate a body-condition assessment. Record your cat’s weight regularly under similar conditions and seek advice if it trends upward or downward unexpectedly.

Kittens need food formulated for growth. Healthy adults generally need an adult-maintenance diet, while senior cats may need changes based on body condition, mobility, dental health or disease. Do not add supplements or switch to a therapeutic diet without veterinary guidance.

Keep fresh, clean water continuously available. Wash bowls regularly and try more than one bowl location or a fountain if that helps your cat drink comfortably.

Grooming and Coat Care

An adult Maine Coon has a two-layered coat that is shorter around the shoulders and longer around the belly, back legs and ruff. Regular combing removes loose hair and finds small tangles before they tighten against the skin. The Cat Fanciers’ Association recommends combing two or three times per week, while TICA emphasizes that some coat textures need more frequent attention.

Use that frequency as a starting point. Work gently with a long-toothed metal comb suitable for a long coat, moving in the direction the hair grows. Give extra attention behind the ears, under the front legs, along the belly, around the chest and on the back legs. Keep sessions short at first and reward calm handling, especially with a kitten.

For a full step-by-step routine covering tools, mats, shedding and bathing, read our complete Maine Coon grooming guide.


Never pull forcefully at a tight mat or place scissors close to the skin. Cat skin can be drawn into a mat and cut accidentally. VCA Animal Hospitals advises using clippers rather than scissors and recommends professional help when tangles are severe or extensive. A veterinarian should assess any redness, wound, odor or skin irritation beneath a mat.

Most healthy adult cats rarely need a bath. Bathe only when the coat is genuinely dirty or when your veterinarian recommends it, and use a product formulated for cats. Comb out minor tangles before wetting the coat because water can make them harder to remove.

Check nails regularly and trim only when needed. Look at the outer ears and around the eyes for changes, but do not insert cotton swabs or cleaning products into the ears unless your veterinarian has shown you what to use. Dental care matters too: ask your veterinary team to demonstrate safe brushing and recommend a realistic home routine.

Exercise, Play and Mental Enrichment

Maine Coons are often described as easygoing, but easygoing does not mean inactive. Daily movement supports muscle condition, helps manage weight and gives a curious cat an appropriate outlet for hunting behavior. Divide interactive play into short sessions that fit your cat’s interest and stamina.

Rotate wand toys, rolling toys and safe objects that can be chased. Puzzle feeders can turn part of a measured meal into a problem-solving activity. Sturdy scratching posts allow stretching, while stable climbing furniture and window perches create vertical territory. Put wand toys, strings and small detachable pieces away after supervised play so they are not chewed or swallowed.

Some Maine Coons enjoy fetch, clicker training, water play or a harness walk, but these are individual preferences rather than breed guarantees. Introduce any new activity gradually and use positive reinforcement. A secure catio can provide outdoor sights and smells without free roaming; a well-fitted harness is another option for a cat that is comfortable wearing one. Never force a fearful cat outdoors.

Watch for changes. A cat that suddenly stops jumping, playing or using stairs may be experiencing pain rather than simply becoming lazy.

Setting Up a Maine Coon-Friendly Home

Choose equipment for the cat your Maine Coon will become, not only the kitten you bring home. A carrier should allow an adult cat to stand, turn and lie down comfortably while remaining structurally secure. Beds and perches need enough usable surface area, and a cat tree should have a wide base, solid joints and platforms that support a large body without wobbling.

Litter boxes are a common weak point. Many standard covered boxes are too cramped for a long cat. FelineVMA’s Cat Friendly Homes guidance says many cats prefer a box about one and a half times their body length. Provide a box that permits easy entry and turning, place it in a quiet accessible location, and scoop it at least daily. In a multicat home, the usual starting rule is one box per cat plus one extra, placed in separate useful locations.

Give your cat a quiet resting place, scratching surfaces in useful positions, separate food and water resources, and safe elevated observation points. Indoor living or secure outdoor access reduces exposure to traffic, fights, predators and infectious risks.

Check the home for hazards: unsecured window screens, toxic plants, exposed cords, hot appliances, medicines, cleaning products and unsafe human foods. Store thread, ribbon, hair ties and wand toys where they cannot be swallowed. Reinspect tall furniture, wall-mounted shelves and climbing equipment regularly as fasteners loosen over time.

Preventive Health and Warning Signs

Routine veterinary care should be individualized rather than copied from a universal calendar. The AAHA/AAFP Feline Life Stage Guidelines explain that a cat’s life stage and lifestyle affect its healthcare plan. Your veterinarian can set the appropriate examination, vaccination, parasite-prevention and dental schedule after considering whether your cat lives indoors, travels, boards, hunts or has contact with other animals.

Maine Coons have recognized predispositions that owners should know about without trying to diagnose at home. These include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), hip dysplasia and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). TICA notes that responsible breeding programs may use DNA testing and echocardiography for HCM, X-rays for hip dysplasia and DNA screening for SMA. Genetic results can provide useful information, but a negative result does not replace physical examinations or other tests recommended by a veterinarian.

Ask a breeder or rescue for available health records and take them to your veterinarian. During ordinary care, pay attention to breathing, appetite, mobility, litter-box habits, weight, grooming ability and behavior. Cats often hide illness, so a persistent change deserves a call to the clinic even when it seems subtle.

Seek urgent veterinary help for difficulty breathing, collapse, sudden inability to stand or use the hind limbs, repeated vomiting with weakness, suspected poisoning, severe lethargy, or straining without passing urine. An extended refusal to eat also needs prompt veterinary advice; do not wait for a routine visit if your cat appears seriously unwell. Call the clinic or emergency hospital while preparing safe transport so its staff can guide you.

Kitten, Adult and Senior Care Differences

Kitten

Maine Coon kitten care begins with growth-formulated food, veterinary guidance for vaccines and parasite control, safe socialization, and gentle handling practice. Introduce the carrier, comb, nail handling, and toothbrushing in short positive sessions. Check equipment frequently as the kitten grows, because a small carrier, litter box or perch may become unsuitable faster than expected.

Adult

For a healthy adult, focus on keeping weight and body condition stable, maintaining the coat, offering daily activity and continuing preventive care. Do not let a busy schedule turn measured meals and interactive play into occasional tasks. Note any gradual changes in jumping, grooming or social behavior and mention them during veterinary visits.

Senior

The 2021 AAHA/AAFP guidelines classify cats aged 10 years and older as senior, although individual aging varies. Make resources easier to reach: consider low-entry litter boxes, non-slip routes, warm resting areas and food and water on the level where the cat spends most of its time. A sturdy step or ramp may help a cat reach a favorite safe perch.

Monitor appetite, drinking, elimination, weight, coat condition, sleep, mobility and interaction more closely. Reduced grooming, missed litter-box visits or reluctance to jump can reflect discomfort or disease, not simply “old age.” Senior cats should receive veterinary examinations at least every six months; cats over 15 or those with chronic conditions may need more frequent visits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Maine Coons hard to take care of?

They are manageable for owners who can provide regular grooming, daily activity, suitable equipment and routine veterinary care. Their long coat and large body create a few extra practical needs, but a predictable schedule prevents most tasks from becoming overwhelming. Individual coat texture and health matter more than the breed label alone.

How often should you groom a Maine Coon?

Start with thorough combing two or three times per week. Increase the frequency if the coat tangles easily or shedding is heavy. Check mat-prone areas during every session. Kittens should be introduced to gentle grooming early, and tight or widespread mats should be handled by a veterinarian or qualified feline groomer.

Our detailed grooming schedule explains how to choose tools, check mat-prone areas and handle small tangles safely.

Do Maine Coons need special food?

They do not automatically need a breed-branded diet. Choose a complete and balanced food for the correct life stage, measure it according to the label and adjust with veterinary guidance based on weight and body condition. Kittens, healthy adults, seniors and cats with medical conditions can have different nutritional needs.

Can a Maine Coon live happily indoors?

Yes. An indoor Maine Coon can thrive when the home provides daily interactive play, scratching areas, sturdy climbing and resting places, clean litter boxes, safe hiding areas and positive social interaction. A secure catio or supervised harness time can add outdoor enrichment, but neither is required for every cat.

What does a Maine Coon need at home?

Start with a secure large carrier, roomy litter box, stable cat tree, strong scratching surfaces, comfortable resting places, food and water stations, grooming tools and varied toys. Check dimensions and weight limits before buying. The best setup gives the cat room to turn, stretch, climb and rest without equipment wobbling or tipping.

A Consistent Routine Makes Maine Coon Care Manageable

A practical routine is simple: provide measured, balanced meals, fresh water, clean litter and play every day; comb the coat several times a week; check nails, weight and equipment regularly; and follow an individualized veterinary plan. Adjust the schedule as your Maine Coon grows and as its coat, body condition, mobility or health changes. Save the care checklist for reference, and discuss diet, grooming difficulties or health concerns with your veterinarian rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all rule.

About the Author

Sami is the founder and editor of Wise Maine Coon. He researches Maine Coon care using reputable veterinary organizations, breed associations and other authoritative sources.
